title: Bath-assisted cooling without resets
authors: Xie-Hang Yu, Zherui Chen, Lin Lin
abstract: Cooling an arbitrary mixed state to a pure ground state requires transferring its entropy to an environment. Can a single coherent bath contact accomplish this without repeated bath resets? We develop a new cooling mechanism that transfers the input information into bath degrees of freedom that subsequently decouple, while the system and the remaining bath follow a ground-state path. The bath is discarded only at the end, and the system Hamiltonian remains on and unmodified throughout. We rigorously realize this mechanism for a class of weakly interacting, gapped fermionic systems with local interactions. Starting from any mixed state, our protocol prepares the interacting ground state in total physical time polylogarithmic in the system size and inverse global trace-norm error. It uses two initially empty bath modes per system mode and a single pulse shared across all onsite system--bath couplings. The same pulse prepares each admissible system's own ground state without knowledge of its microscopic parameters. The guarantees follow directly from a non-Markovian system--bath dynamics without an effective Lindbladian description.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, single-contact quantum cooling mechanism to prepare a system's ground state from any mixed state. It achieves this by coherently transferring entropy into a bath that is only discarded at the end, avoiding the need for repeated resets. The protocol is rigorously proven for gapped fermionic systems and operates in polylogarithmic time.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of cooling an arbitrary mixed quantum state to its pure ground state by transferring entropy to an environment (bath) without requiring repeated bath resets.
main_result: A novel, single-contact, non-Markovian cooling protocol is rigorously developed that achieves ground-state preparation in polylogarithmic physical time relative to system size and desired accuracy.
method: The method involves designing a time-dependent, coherent system-bath coupling Hamiltonian that guides the system through three controlled stages: Entrance, Transport, and Exit.
model_or_system: The analysis is applied to weakly interacting, gapped fermionic systems on a lattice, modeled by a system Hamiltonian $H_u$ coupled to an environment bath via $H_{SE}(t)$.
key_observables: The primary observable is the fidelity of the final state $ho_{out}$ to the true ground state $|Gangle$, quantified by the trace-norm error $\epsilon$.
important_parameters: The time scale $	au$ scales polylogarithmically with $N/\epsilon$, and the control strength must be parametrically larger than the local energy scale $\Lambda$ of the system.
main_assumptions: The system Hamiltonian must be geometrically local and gapped, and the analysis relies on bounding errors across multiple sequential, controlled evolution stages.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares previous multi-round cooling protocols with the proposed single continuous joint evolution. Figure 2 illustrates the three-stage control path (Entrance, Transport, Exit) governing the time-dependent coupling.
paper_structure: The paper develops the protocol by defining the total Hamiltonian, detailing the three sequential control stages (Entrance, Transport, Exit) required for the evolution, and finally providing rigorous mathematical bounds on the accumulated leakage and error across these stages.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controlled, non-Markovian framework for quantum state preparation, which is crucial for implementing quantum simulations or quantum computation protocols where state purity is paramount.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Two organizations of cooling. Left: previous repeated cooling rounds with freshly reset bath modes can realize a dissipative evolution. Right: we design one continuous joint evolution with a finite coherent bath. The system approaches its interacting ground state for every input ρS, while the bath retains the input entropy and information. The distinction lies in the joint dynamics during the system–bath evolution.

FIG. 2. Three-stage cooling control path (A(t), ω(t)) in the rotating frame. The numbered points on the control path connect to the corresponding stage diagrams. Entrance transfers input entropy to the dark sector; transport follows the system–bright ground-state branch while the dark sector remains decoupled; exit releases the system and discards the bath. The state labels describe the ideal limit.
